To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a Mr 150000 surface glycoprotein is involved in protein-mediated adhesion of adult hepatocytes.
a 150 kDa surface protein is involved in the attachment of adult hepatocyte to protein substrates.

a Mr 150,000 glycoprotein is redistributed to the surface of hepatocytes in the presence of protein substrates and is increased beneath cells when the protein-mediated attachment is markedly enhanced.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of a surface protein that may mediate protein-mediated attachment of cultured hepatocytes.
the identification of the surface glycoproteins that are involved in the adhesion process.

the molecular mechanisms of protein-mediated cell adhesion, with the aim of understanding how cell adhesion and cell-substratum interactions are involved in the control of cell growth, differentiation, and morphogenesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Mr 150 00 surface protein is a key component in protein-mediated attachment of hepatocytes and that the attachment change is mediated by a redistribution of this protein into the cell-substrate contact area.
the attachment of adult Wistar hepatocytes is controlled by the redistribution of a surface glyco- protein in the cell membrane.
the surface glycoprotein may have a regulatory role in the adhesion of adult hepatocytes to protein-coated substrata.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the surface glycoprotein is an important determinant of the attachment of hepatocytes to proteins.
the Mr 150 00 surface protein may play a role in controlling cell adhesion to protein substrates and that this may involve its association with other membrane components.

the surface of the hepatocyte is a dynamic structure that changes in response to the environment and that the changes in the cell surface are accompanied by changes in the cell-substratum interactions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have developed a method that allows for the isolation of the surface glycoprotein from hepatocytes and the subsequent identification of the glycosylation pattern on the surface of hepatocytes.
the attachment change is mediated by an increase in the amount of a surface glycosylated protein, which may be involved in the formation and/or stabilization of cell-substrate contact areas.
this surface glycoprotein may play a critical role in the control of cell adhesion to protein substrates.
